drugRefs.why: Oral (not IV) vancomycin is first-line for C. difficile infection - it acts locally in the gut lumen and is not systemically absorbed, which is precisely why it works here despite IV vancomycin having no role in typical gut infections.

drugRefs.coverage: Associated with lower recurrence rates than vancomycin per current IDSA guidance; cost and availability often limit use.

drugRefs.regimenLabel: Metronidazole (only if vancomycin/fidaxomicin unavailable, non-severe disease)
drugRefs.coverage: No longer preferred first-line per current guidelines given inferior efficacy compared to vancomycin, but remains an option where the other agents are inaccessible.

coverageMatrix.completeness: Either agent provides effective coverage of the causative organism when given correctly (oral route, adequate duration).
gaps: IV vancomycin does NOT treat C. difficile colitis - this is a critical distinction, since IV vancomycin does not reach adequate concentrations in the gut lumen.

stewardship.deescalation: Not typically applicable in the de-escalation sense since therapy is already targeted; reassess for fulminant disease if not improving, which would escalate rather than narrow therapy.

framework: Discontinue the inciting antibiotic if it is still being given and is not essential - this alone can resolve milder cases.
Avoid antimotility agents (e.g., loperamide), which can precipitate toxic megacolon.

For fulminant disease (ileus, megacolon, shock), oral vancomycin should be combined with IV metronidazole and surgical consultation - this is the one scenario where IV metronidazole plays a role alongside oral vancomycin.
This is a uniquely 'reverse stewardship' scenario: the treatment is itself an antibiotic, so the focus is on correct route/agent selection (oral, not IV vancomycin) rather than withholding therapy.
